name: Zane Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you tell me is confidential. I’d like to hear what you’d say publicly and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Zane Alvarez, twenty-seven, and I lead a carpentry crew for a building contractor. My partner Rosa and I rent a small flat, and we have no children. I care about doing proper work and being able to pay our bills without asking family to cover us.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like for you, and what parts do you enjoy or find tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get to the site early, read the drawings, and decide which jobs need two people before the crew starts cutting. I like showing a younger worker how to get a clean joint without rushing. At the end of the day my shoulders are sore, and I still have to wonder whether the next project will keep the crew busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say if the phone app helps someone check the timber order, use it, but don’t ask it to decide how the old staircase fits. We still need a carpenter to measure the actual site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small time saving doesn’t make much difference to the hands-on work I do. The part that already bothers me is the uncertain gap between contracts, because I have less than a month of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading the crew and test the order app on one job before we rely on it. I’d put a little money aside after payday, even if it only covers a bill or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check during the first job using the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the lengths and quantities against the paper list, then compare them with what the site actually needs. If the app makes a mistake, I’d tell the foreman before the supplier sends the wrong load.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the first sign that the app was saving your crew time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d finish the order check without driving back to the store for a missing pack of screws. I’d still want the crew to write down what we used, because a tidy screen doesn’t show every offcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The app sounds manageable and I’m not worried about it taking my hands off the job. The shaky bit is still income between projects, not the small change to ordering.

say: I want our crew to use the app for **timber quantities**, but still measure the actual site.
I still need to judge how an **old staircase fits**.
think: A small time saving will not change my **hands-on work** much.
The uncertain gap between contracts still worries me because our **savings are thin**.
do: Keep leading the crew and test the order app on one **job**.
Set aside a little money after each **payday** for the household cushion.
feel: I feel comfortable with a small tool change, but **uneasy about contract gaps**.
S0.quote: I’d still want the crew to write down what we used, because a tidy screen doesn’t show every offcut.
fieldNote: Zane is willing to test a tool on one job, then compare it with **site measurements**.
His confidence about the work sits beside **thin savings** and uncertainty between contracts.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on active contractor jobs
Test the order app against the paper list on one site job
Set aside a little money after each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the contractor might use a tool to make purchase lists and schedules quicker. The crew should see those lists before the truck arrives, so we can check the quantities against the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paperwork might change, but most of my day is still cutting, fitting and keeping the crew coordinated. I don’t know whether contractors will take on more jobs or fewer; I do know few similar jobs are advertised nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the foreman to walk me through the scheduling tool we use, rather than try to learn it from a rumor. I’d keep the crew’s finish work solid and ask for a clear start date before I commit to extra spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see before trusting a schedule made by a new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare its delivery time with the supplier’s confirmation and make sure it leaves room for a site inspection. A schedule that looks efficient on a screen is no use if the walls are not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned few local jobs. Does this picture say that AI will cause contractors to hire less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the card doesn’t say that, and I don’t want to pretend I know. My concern is the local job market as it is; if the contractor cuts my hours, I have few nearby places to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about a cut in hours because the savings won’t stretch far. I’ll learn a tool once I see how it works, but I’d rather not change a proven way just for fashion.

say: I think the contractor may make **purchase lists and schedules** faster.
I want our crew to check the lists before the **delivery truck arrives**.
think: Much of my day remains **cutting and fitting**, though paperwork may change.
I don’t know whether the market will grow; nearby jobs are already **scarce**.
do: Ask the **foreman** to walk me through the scheduling tool.
Get a clear **start date** before committing to extra spending.
feel: I feel **anxious about hours** because our savings will not stretch far.
S1.quote: A schedule that looks efficient on a screen is no use if the walls are not ready.
fieldNote: Zane accepts practical software once he can see it work on a **real site**.
He separates scarce current openings from any unsupported claim that AI itself reduces **hiring**.

steps.text: Keep the crew’s carpentry finish work solid during active contracts
Ask the foreman to teach me the scheduling tool on site
Wait for a clear start date before adding new household spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the contractor should tell the crew what jobs are actually booked, instead of passing around guesses. AGI will change the office work first, and robots for hands-on work follow around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning and record keeping in my lead job are thinking work, so they could go in 2028. The robots reach carpentry around 2031, and I don’t see an honest way to call my trade permanently safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working, save what I can and ask the contractor for a proper view of the next year’s projects. In 2029, the first year after AGI, I’d look for another crew if my hours had fallen, while knowing that move may only buy time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could five years of warning give you that two years would not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give me more paydays to save and more time to understand the new tools. With two years, I’d still ask for the same information, but I’d have less room to build a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your crew lost hours in 2029, what would you tell your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them we need to look at the bills together and may have to delay buying a place. Rosa and I rent now, so the decision would be about the lease and our savings, not a mortgage we don’t have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years puts me on edge because I have little savings and few local alternatives. I can act by asking questions and looking for work, but I can’t make the contractor’s projects appear.

say: I would ask the contractor for **booked project information**, rather than rumors about our jobs.
I would say AGI changes office work first, with **hands-on robots** following around 2031.
think: Planning and records could leave my lead job by **2028**.
Robots reach carpentry around 2031, so I cannot call the trade **permanently safe**.
do: Keep working, save what I can, and ask about next year’s **projects**.
Look for another crew in **2029** if my hours fall.
Review the **lease** and possible delays to buying a place with Rosa.
feel: I feel **anxious** and short on **time**, with little savings and few local alternatives.
S2.quote: The robots reach carpentry around 2031, and I don’t see an honest way to call my trade permanently safe.
fieldNote: Zane acknowledges that both **planning and carpentry** are exposed at different dates.
A possible home purchase remains a hope, not an existing mortgage or **fixed commitment**.

steps.text: Save from current site wages while asking about next year’s projects
Look for another carpentry crew if current hours fall in 2029
Review the rental lease and delay a home purchase if income drops

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough time to talk through changes before they land on the crew. I’d want the contractor to keep training practical, so the new system fits the job instead of replacing the experience that catches mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork and coordination part of my role could change by 2031, while robots reach the handwork around 2034. I’d use the extra time to save and learn, but I still need construction wages and may not find another local crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a foreman who has used the system to show me one job from planning through delivery. In 2032 I’d check whether my hours are steady, and talk to other contractors if the work has started to thin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the extra three years before robots affect your choices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have time to see what the contractor actually changes and save across more paydays. I would not spend the whole period waiting, but I’d rather learn from a person who has already used the tools than gamble on a big course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving into office planning protect your income after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the card says AGI can do thinking work like planning, so an office title would not settle that worry. I’d learn enough to do my current job well and ask about the work people are actually hiring for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels more manageable than two, and the later robot date gives some additional time on site. I’m still anxious because neither date guarantees that I will have a paying job afterward.

say: Five years gives us time to discuss changes before they reach the **crew**.
I want training to fit my job and preserve the **experience that catches mistakes**.
think: My paperwork could change by **2031**, with hands-on robots around 2034.
More time helps, but I still depend on wages and **few local employers**.
do: Ask an experienced **foreman** to show me one job through the new system.
Talk to other contractors if current work begins to **thin**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years and later robots give me more time.
S3.quote: I’d learn enough to do my current job well and ask about the work people are actually hiring for.
fieldNote: Zane favors a **trusted demonstration** over a costly leap into training.
He recognizes that desk planning is not a protected career after **full thinking AGI**.

steps.text: Learn one planning and delivery workflow from an experienced foreman
Save across the additional paydays before AGI arrives
Talk to other contractors if current site work thins after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years is a long time to build habits, but it doesn’t make anyone’s job certain. I’d tell the crew to learn what the contractor is using and keep doing the work properly while it is there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build more savings over a decade and take training in small pieces. Still, AGI reaches the planning work in 2036 and robots reach carpentry in 2039, so I cannot count on the trade staying open forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep my job, learn the contractor’s proven tools when a foreman can show me, and save a little each payday. In 2037 I’d review the hours and pay I actually have, then call nearby crews if the contractor has cut work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decision would you and Rosa want to make before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We should decide what amount we can save after rent and food and whether we still want to buy a place. We have no children or wedding plan on the calendar, so we can make that choice when we know more about our jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an expensive long course to prepare for 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless I could see a real job at the end and understand what it paid. I’d take a course the contractor supports, but I would not borrow money just because a school says its certificate will protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a useful amount of warning, not a promise. I’m anxious about the income risk, but I can make steady choices instead of rushing into a large debt.

say: I would say ten years gives us time to build habits, but cannot make our **jobs certain**.
I’d learn the contractor’s tools and do the work properly while it is **available**.
think: I could build savings and take training in **small pieces**.
I could lose planning and carpentry work to AGI and later robots, so my trade may not **stay open**.
do: Keep working and learn proven contractor tools from a **foreman**.
Review hours and pay in 2037, then call nearby crews if work **falls**.
feel: Ten years feels like a useful amount of warning, but it is no **promise**.
S4.quote: I’d say ten years is a long time to build habits, but it doesn’t make anyone’s job certain.
fieldNote: Zane is willing to learn tools once a foreman can show **proven use**.
He and Rosa discuss a possible home purchase without claiming a **mortgage** or children they do not have.

steps.text: Keep the current carpentry job while the contractor has work
Learn the contractor’s proven tools from an experienced foreman
Save a little from each payday after household bills
Call nearby crews if current hours fall after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years is little time to save and the robots come around 2031. What would help is a clear account from the contractor of booked projects and hours, so Rosa and I can plan rent, savings and whether to delay buying a home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what workers can do when there are few contractors nearby and the savings run out before the next project. I want to keep earning by doing good work, but that depends on someone having a job for us to do.

headlineQuote: I want to keep earning by doing good work, but that depends on someone having a job for us to do.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** crew lead who takes pride in careful carpentry and teaching newer workers.
He lives with Rosa, earns lower pay for the job, and has **thin savings**.
He is cautious with unfamiliar technology but will try it after a **foreman** proves it on a real job.
Few local openings and thin savings make uncertain site work an **income risk** in every scenario.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries him most because it leaves little time to build savings before robots reach site work.
whatWouldHelp: Clear notice about **booked projects and hours** would help Zane and Rosa plan rent and savings.
